product: Startup Launch Agents (LLC formation, name, website, compliance)
owner_brief:
Thank you for the answers. All five confirmed the defaults already in the plan, so nothing changed there: each founder approves only their own 83(b), sites publish to Netlify, an edit after approval makes everyone sign again, vesting starts on the incorporation date, and websites get Home, About, Services and Contact unless the founder asks otherwise.

What I changed. The product is now planned as something you can sell, not a demo. Founders get real accounts (sign up, log in, reset a password, confirm their email) and invite co-founders by email; everyone sees only their own companies and can act only as themselves. The "act as founder" switch survives only in demo mode. Approving a document becomes a proper electronic signature: you type your full name, tick a consent box, and we record the time, your account, your IP address and a fingerprint of the exact text. Signed documents download as a PDF with a signature page, plus an editable Word copy for filling in addresses and tax IDs offline. Plans and payments run through Stripe (test mode until you switch on live keys). Emails go out for invites, signatures and the 83(b) deadline at 14, 7 and 2 days. There is a landing page, pricing, Terms, Privacy, data export and account deletion, and a small admin area that shows account information but never your customers' documents. Behind the scenes: PostgreSQL in production, Docker, automatic checks on every change, limits on login attempts and AI use, removal of tax IDs typed into the chat, and background jobs so nothing hangs. All the shared rules for this sit in the very first round, so later rounds only add features.

The AI is one setting. On your own computer the agents can use your Claude Code login (no API key); the app warns that this is for your own use only and refuses to start in production. Production uses an Anthropic API key with Claude Opus 5.5 by default, and a cheaper model per agent if you want (for example Haiku for the Name and QA agents). If Claude declines a request on safety grounds, it automatically retries on a fallback model. DeepSeek and Groq stay available.

The demo video is a real feature. One command drives the actual app at 1920x1080 with a caption per step and shows each agent's output: the case summary, a legal answer and the three document types, name cards with domain badges, the cap table with chart and Excel file, signing with a cancelled-and-redone signature, the website preview with its QA report and live link (or "packaged"), and the registration checklist. Each run saves WebM and MP4 videos, a screenshot per step and every file the agents made. "Reliable" mode is offline and identical every run; "live" mode uses real AI, real domain checks and real publishing. It must pass three times in a row before it counts as done.

What you'll see after each round. The plan grew from 23 to 46 pieces in 7 rounds. Round 0 is groundwork. After round 1 you can open the design gallery with the brand in light and dark mode; behind it twenty pieces work on their own (rules, saving, agents, AI connections, accounts, email, payments, background jobs, PDFs, security). Round 2 joins them into the conversation, website, legal, email and admin services. Round 3 makes the whole backend available and secured. After round 4 every screen works, from the landing page to the admin area, and the product runs in Docker. Round 5 tests the full customer journey and adds a guide to running it. Round 6 records the demo video.

What I need from you. 1) Answer three questions: pricing, the product name, and what happens to shared companies when someone deletes their account. Each already has a recommended answer in the plan. 2) Have the operator install seven Python packages before building starts: alembic, psycopg[binary], argon2-cffi, stripe, reportlab, python-docx and email-validator. The web app's few new form and control packages install automatically. 3) Have the operator add a link to the demo-video instructions in the main README, which only the operator may edit. 4) Before going live (not needed for building): an Anthropic API key; a Stripe account with a monthly and a yearly price and a webhook secret; an email-sending (SMTP) account with a verified sending domain; a Netlify token; a web address with HTTPS for the app; and your legal company name, contact email and governing-law state for the Terms and Privacy pages, which ship as marked drafts for your lawyer to review.

waves.goal: Groundwork: the shared vocabulary of the product, the contracts for accounts, billing, email and background jobs, the database layout, and stand-ins for the AI and every outside service, so twenty pieces can be built at the same time next. Nothing to look at yet.

Twenty pieces built side by side: the automatic rules (equity, vesting, 83(b), cap table, approvals), saving to SQLite and PostgreSQL, the five specialist agents, the AI connections (your own Claude Code login on your machine, the Anthropic API for production), accounts and co-founder invites, email, Stripe billing, background jobs, signed PDFs, security and logging, and the app's look and feel. You can open the design gallery and see the brand in light and dark mode.

The services that join it all up: the Manager conversation with hand-overs, the website build-check-publish pipeline, the company and legal services with electronic signatures, signature and 83(b) reminder emails, data export and account deletion, and the admin service.
The complete, secured backend: every endpoint checks who you are and what you may do; sign-up, billing, team, chat, legal and website all work over the API; ready-made demo companies at every stage.

Every screen: landing and pricing, sign-up and onboarding, chat and overview, names and domains, legal e-signing, cap table, website, registration guide, settings with billing and team, and the admin area, each checked in a real browser; plus Docker with PostgreSQL and automatic checks on every change.
The whole customer journey, from the landing page and payment to a finished company kit, tested end to end, plus a plain guide to running the product.
The demo video: one command records every agent at work, in reliable mode (identical every run) or live mode (real AI, real domain checks, real publishing).

open_questions.question: Who needs to approve each founder's 83(b) tax election form?
open_questions.why_it_matters: The 83(b) form is a personal tax filing for one founder. It decides whose approval is needed before the legal step counts as complete.

options.label: Only that founder
options.description: Each founder approves just their own 83(b). This matches how the IRS form works and means fewer clicks.

options.label: All founders
options.description: Every founder approves every 83(b) form. This follows the brief word for word but adds clicks and has no legal effect.

open_questions.question: Which hosting service should publish the founder's website?
open_questions.why_it_matters: It decides which account and token you need for live publishing, and what the site's address looks like (for example crumb-ledger.netlify.app).

options.label: Netlify
options.description: Free tier, one upload puts the site live with HTTPS in about a minute. You'd add a Netlify token.

options.label: Cloudflare Pages
options.description: Fast and free, but more build work on our side. You'd need a Cloudflare account and token.

options.label: Vercel
options.description: Popular, with similar extra build work to Cloudflare. You'd need a Vercel token.

open_questions.question: Can a founder still edit a document after every founder has approved it?
open_questions.why_it_matters: It decides whether signed documents are final, or whether a late change reopens them for everyone to approve again.

options.label: Yes, everyone re-approves
options.description: The edit creates a new version, cancels the other approvals, and marks the legal step incomplete until everyone approves again.

options.label: No, signed is final
options.description: Approved documents are locked. Any change means generating new documents. Safer, but less flexible.

open_questions.question: When does founder vesting start?
open_questions.why_it_matters: It sets every date on the vesting timeline, the cliff date, and the date each founder is fully vested.

options.label: On the incorporation date
options.description: No extra question for the founder. This is standard for brand-new companies.

options.label: Ask for a start date
options.description: The Manager asks one more question. Useful when founders worked together before incorporating.

open_questions.question: Which pages should the website have when the founder doesn't say?
open_questions.why_it_matters: It shapes every generated site and what the QA Agent checks for.

options.label: Home, About, Services, Contact
options.description: A classic four-page small-business site that looks complete and professional.

options.label: One long page
options.description: A single scrolling page with all sections. Simpler, but it can feel less established.

open_questions.question: How should founders pay for the product, and how much?
open_questions.why_it_matters: It decides what the pricing page says, what is free, what needs a paid plan, and whether founders have a subscription to cancel. Prices are settings, so changing them later is easy; changing the model (subscription or one-time) is more work.

options.label: Free + $39/month
options.description: A free plan to try everything except documents, e-signing and publishing; the Launch plan at $39 a month or $390 a year unlocks them. Cancel anytime in the billing portal.

options.label: One-time $249 per company
options.description: Pay once per company for everything, no subscription. Simpler for founders, but no recurring revenue for ongoing reminders and hosting help.

options.label: Three tiers
options.description: Free, Launch $29/month and Team $79/month (more companies and AI messages, priority support). More choice, more to explain on the pricing page.

options.label: Paid only, 14-day trial
options.description: No free plan: $49 a month after a 14-day trial. Fewer free users to support, but a higher barrier to trying it.

open_questions.question: What should the product be called?
open_questions.why_it_matters: The name appears on every page, in every email and on every signed PDF. It is one setting, so we build with a working name now and can switch later, but the landing page, logo and web address depend on it.

options.label: Charterly
options.description: Friendly and memorable; a company charter is a founding document. We check the domain and trademark before launch.

options.label: Foundwell
options.description: Suggests a company that is well founded; warm and simple.

options.label: LaunchDesk
options.description: Plain and descriptive: the desk where you launch your company. Easy to understand, harder to trademark.

options.label: Keep "Launch Agents"
options.description: The current working title; describes the AI agents, but sounds more like a tool than a brand.

open_questions.question: When a founder deletes their account, what happens to a company they share with co-founders?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Signed founding documents are a legal record the other founders still need, but the person leaving also expects their data to go away.

options.label: Company stays with co-founders
options.description: The company and its signed documents stay with the others (the departed founder's typed signature remains as the record); companies only they belong to are deleted.

options.label: Block until handed over
options.description: The founder must leave or hand over each shared company first; deletion works only once nothing is shared. Safer, one more step for the user.

options.label: Delete everything they touched
options.description: Removes the founder's messages and signatures from shared companies too. Their co-founders would lose part of their signed record.
